What about security specifically are you wondering about? Most distributions comes with iptables as it's firewall, which is a stateful inspecting firewall allowing you to fine grain the packet analysis down to keywords found in the packet if need be, and allows for rerouting of traffic to different devices. Some distros use SELinux as its ACL's. Depending on what filesystem you use, there are permissions that can be applied to devices and partitions (for example, chattr for ext3/4 filesystems). Now that Linux is starting to gain in popularity, there are now anti-virus programs out there like AVG and ClamAV to help protect against malware. Browser based threats are still protected against by Firefox and Chrome's ad blockers and malicious site checking.

Hardware compatibility is usually good. While there are still some wireless devices that have issues, most do not. Graphics cards are fine, though the AMD proprietary drivers aren't the best, if you are not a serious gamer it shouldn't affect you. Some sound card chipsets can be a problem but for the most part, all built in sound cards found on the motherboard will work. It really seems like the more niche a device is, the less likely it will be supported in Linux. Most printers will work, the only exceptions really seem to be the 4-in-1 printers. They usually require special programs from the manufacturer to work. But, if you buy a stand alone printer, stand alone scanner, etc. they should pretty much work out of the box without the need to install special drivers.

You can do with it exactly what you use your Windows computer for.

I use a fine distribution called Arch Linux. I prefer it because:

  1. It comes with nothing but the bare essentials, and a package manager. This means you chose your software. It also doesn't come with an installer so you chose how to install it completely. It's about as configurable as it gets without compiling everything manually.
  2. The package manger (called 'Pacman') is a lot more intuitive than Aptitude, which is the package manager most distributions use.
  3. The Arch user repository makes getting software that couldn't be put in the official repos easy.
  4. The distribution has famously good documentation.
  5. The biggest reason: It is rolling release. This means that after a system update you are always using the most resent version of the operating system. Most operating systems are released in versions, and upgrading versions is often hard. Not on Arch, just run pacman -Syu and your done.

It is my favorite operating system for these reasons and more.

Both of these have GREAT support and use the Advanced Package Tools system, so just about any instructions for Ubuntu will apply for LM or Elementary. This means you will have support for any and every problem you run into... which brings me to the next thing: Don't listen to users like /u/Wargasm.

1) Yes, he's right about video games... Linux isn't the best, but they really haven't been trying until the last 18 months. But, in that 18 months, it's grown in leaps and bounds due to Steam.

2) LibreOffice/OpenOffice can edit and save MSOffice documents. Yes, you may run into formatting issues from time to time, but these are still compatible, unlike Wargasm put things. He makes it sound like it's impossible, and that's just not the case. I usually save things as a PDF, which retains all formats, which is what anyone would do if they're doing a professional presentation... or load it onto a Microsoft machine and tweak the little things that change, before the presentation, when I check my work beforehand (who goes into a presentation cold?).

3) The support point is an outright lie. Unless you're using Arch or Gentoo (which are reserved for "advanced" users who should know what they're doing), you're going to find support and walkthroughs for anything and everything you need. If you're having a problem, you're definitely not the first and SOMEONE has found the solution to it. Check the forums if you don't believe me... everything from changing the clock format to partitioning drives... You can literally find anything and everything. The community and support are the things that keep people around. Again, if you're trying Arch or Gentoo, don't be surprised to find a lot of "check the manual" responses, but that's not the case for Linux in general.

4) I have multiple Linux machines running multiple distros, built on a wide range of hardware, and I have yet to find something that doesn't work. Intel chipsets, NVIDIA GPU, AMD processors... everything works. As stated in bullet #3, you may run into compatibility issues with Arch/Gentoo, but that's because of the way it's designed... You're supposed to work through incompatibility yourself. But every other distro has a team behind it, finding these incompatibilities and working them out before releasing the updates to users. This is literally a nonissue for you, unlike Wargasm puts it.

I also wouldn't suggest LiLi to create a live USB... it's pretty, but it's also bloated and unnecessarily so. I'd suggest Universal USB Installer or Rufus as they're more refined and straightforward... LiLi is Vista as UUI is Windows 7, as I like to put it.

And, while a live USB is a way to try the OS, you should take it with a grain of salt. Your USB is going to be slow reading and writing, so the OS will be too. It'll seem buggy and jittery at times because you're running from a USB stick instead of a SATA hard drive.

I'd recommend using the USB stick to create a partition on your current system to preserve Windows/OSX and run it side-by-side with Linux. This'll give you the chance to REALLY try Linux out. And, if you decide it's not for you, you can remove the partition and re-expand Windows/OSX and you're back to where you are now... no harm no foul.

As for security, it's MUCH more secure than Windows/OSX. I'm not going to shoot you the line of shit telling you that there aren't any viruses or malware for Linux, because there is... but the way files are structured, everything needs a password (or a login for a certain user) to be accessed. Most of the time you won't notice this, but it's there and it makes things more secure than the alternatives.

And, if you're still afraid, I'd be more than happy to help you try things out. I have run the gamut of distros and have loved/hated each one.
